lines.t: Evolution is usually reconstructed after the fact, from fossils and from the DNA of the survivors.
But what if we could watch it happen, live, in a flask, and follow every family of cells as it rises or falls?
That is the promise of an evolution experiment.
The recipe is simple. Start with an ancestor: a single clone, so every cell begins genetically identical.
Place it in an environment that poses a challenge. Here, a medium in which glucose, the yeast's favourite food, runs out.
Let it grow for hundreds or thousands of generations. Yeast in these experiments manage about eight generations every two days.
A thousand human generations take about twenty-five thousand years. For this yeast, about eight months.
Keep a frozen fossil record. Samples stored at minus eighty degrees can be revived, so the past can be compared directly with the present.
Run replicates, and you can ask which parts of evolution repeat, and which are chance.
The most common format is serial batch transfer.
Cells go into fresh medium, wake up, and divide exponentially, fermenting glucose.
When the glucose is gone, they switch to respiring the ethanol they made, and growth slows to a crawl.
Every 48 hours, 400 µL of the 100 mL culture moves into a fresh flask: a 1-in-250 dilution.
lines.say: Every forty-eight hours, four hundred microlitres of the hundred-millilitre culture move into a fresh flask: a one-in-two-hundred-fifty dilution.

lines.t: 250 is roughly 2⁸, so each cycle is about eight generations of growth.
lines.say: Two hundred fifty is roughly two to the eighth power, so each cycle is about eight generations of growth.

lines.t: The bottleneck still carries tens of millions of cells. The leftovers go into the freezer.
Meanwhile, every division risks a copying error. Most mutations do nothing or do harm. A rare few let cells grow faster.
A mutant just 5% fitter grows exponentially relative to everyone else, and can eventually take over.
lines.say: A mutant just five percent fitter grows exponentially relative to everyone else, and can eventually take over.

lines.t: Here is the catch. Sequencing a whole population only reveals mutations that are already common, roughly 1% or more.
lines.say: Here is the catch. Sequencing a whole population only reveals mutations that are already common, roughly one percent or more.

lines.t: By then the race is mostly over. Thousands of beneficial mutations arose and competed far below that line.
Most are lost to chance while still rare, or are outcompeted by fitter neighbours. This is clonal interference.
To truly see evolution, we would need to follow every lineage from its first cell. We would need to give every cell a name.
That name is a DNA barcode.
A barcode is a short stretch of random DNA, about twenty letters, inserted at the same neutral spot in every cell's genome.
With four possible letters at each of twenty positions, there are over a trillion possible sequences, so two cells almost never share one.
The barcode does nothing for the cell. It does not change fitness. But it is copied every time the cell divides.
So every descendant inherits the same tag. A barcode marks a lineage: an entire family of cells.
And because every barcode sits between the same fixed sequences, all of them can be read at once: amplify with PCR, sequence, and count.
lines.say: And because every barcode sits between the same fixed sequences, all of them can be read at once: amplify with P C R, sequence, and count.

lines.t: Levy and colleagues built this system in baker's yeast in 2015. First, they engineered a landing pad into the genome.
lines.say: Levy and colleagues built this system in baker's yeast in twenty fifteen. First, they engineered a landing pad into the genome.

lines.t: It carries the Cre recombinase gene, switched on by galactose, half of the URA3 gene, and a modified lox site.
lines.say: It carries the Cree recombinase gene, switched on by galactose, half of the U R A 3 gene, and a modified lox site.

lines.t: Next, a plasmid library: each plasmid with its own random barcode, the other half of URA3, and a partner lox site.
lines.say: Next, a plasmid library: each plasmid with its own random barcode, the other half of U R A 3, and a partner lox site.

lines.t: On galactose, cells make Cre, which recombines the two lox sites and stitches the plasmid into the chromosome.
lines.say: On galactose, cells make Cree, which recombines the two lox sites and stitches the plasmid into the chromosome.

lines.t: The two URA3 halves join into one working gene, with the barcode inside an artificial intron that is spliced out.
lines.say: The two U R A 3 halves join into one working gene, with the barcode inside an artificial intron that is spliced out.

lines.t: Only integrated cells can grow without uracil. And one of the new lox sites is doubly mutated, so Cre can barely pull the barcode back out.
lines.say: Only integrated cells can grow without uracil. And one of the new lox sites is doubly mutated, so Cree can barely pull the barcode back out.

lines.t: The result: about half a million yeast lineages, each carrying its own unique barcode.
At every transfer, cells left over after the bottleneck are frozen. Later, their DNA is extracted and the barcode region is amplified by PCR.
lines.say: At every transfer, cells left over after the bottleneck are frozen. Later, their DNA is extracted and the barcode region is amplified by P C R.

lines.t: Each primer carries a random unique molecular identifier, so copies of the same original molecule are counted only once.
Sample-specific index sequences let many time points share a single sequencing run.
Millions of reads are matched to known barcodes. Counting them gives the frequency of every lineage at every time point.
A barcode's frequency over time is a lineage's life story.
Two replicate populations, E1 and E2, evolved under glucose limitation for about 168 generations, sampled every eight.
lines.say: Two replicate populations, E one and E two, evolved under glucose limitation for about one hundred sixty-eight generations, sampled every eight.

lines.t: At first every lineage is tiny, about two cells in a million. As the population improves, neutral lineages slowly decline.
But some lineages bend upward. Each rising line carries a beneficial mutation.
From each curve's shape, the authors inferred two numbers: how much fitter the mutant is, and when the mutation arose.
In replicate E1, about 25,000 lineages carried beneficial mutations worth more than 2%.
lines.say: In replicate E one, about twenty-five thousand lineages carried beneficial mutations worth more than two percent.

lines.t: Mutations worth more than 5% arose at roughly one per million cells per generation.
lines.say: Mutations worth more than five percent arose at roughly one per million cells per generation.

lines.t: Most benefits were small, 2 to 5%, but the distribution was not a simple exponential. It had bumps at larger effects.
lines.say: Most benefits were small, two to five percent, but the distribution was not a simple exponential. It had bumps at larger effects.

lines.t: Many adaptive mutations were already present at the start, arising during the growth that followed barcoding.
Whole-population sequencing would have caught perhaps fifteen of them.
Next, thousands of barcoded clones were isolated, and hundreds were whole-genome sequenced by Venkataram and colleagues in 2016.
lines.say: Next, thousands of barcoded clones were isolated, and hundreds were whole-genome sequenced by Venkataram and colleagues in twenty sixteen.

lines.t: Many had simply doubled their genome and become diploid. Most others carried a single mutation in a nutrient-sensing pathway.
Above all Ras/PKA, with hits in IRA1, IRA2, GPB2 and PDE2, all brakes on the pathway, plus a few in TOR/Sch9.
lines.say: Above all, Ras P K A, with hits in I R A 1, I R A 2, G P B 2 and P D E 2, all brakes on the pathway, plus a few in TOR, S C H 9.

lines.t: Hundreds of distinct mutations, but only a handful of genes, and essentially two pathways.
So do these adaptive mutants all change the same few traits? In 2020, Kinsler, Geiler-Samerotte and Petrov set out to ask.
lines.say: So do these adaptive mutants all change the same few traits? In twenty twenty, Kinsler, Geiler-Samerotte and Petrov set out to ask.

lines.t: Because each mutant is barcoded, all of their fitnesses can be measured at once, in one flask.
A pool of barcoded mutants is mixed with the ancestral reference strain, which makes up 90% of the cells.
lines.say: A pool of barcoded mutants is mixed with the ancestral reference strain, which makes up ninety percent of the cells.

lines.t: Each mutant competes against the ancestor, and the population's average fitness barely moves.
The pool is propagated as in the evolution: 48-hour cycles, about fifty million cells per transfer, five time points.
lines.say: The pool is propagated as in the evolution: forty-eight-hour cycles, about fifty million cells per transfer, five time points.

lines.t: The reference barcode carries a restriction site, so it is cut away before sequencing, saving reads for the mutants.
Fitness is the slope of each barcode's log frequency over time, corrected for mean fitness, which is tracked with neutral lineages.
They measured 292 adaptive mutants in 45 environments.
lines.say: They measured two hundred ninety-two adaptive mutants in forty-five environments.

lines.t: Nine were repeats of the original evolution condition. The rest nudged it: more glucose, a baffled flask, shorter or longer transfers, salt, or drugs.
Variation between the repeats set the yardstick for what counts as a subtle perturbation.
Twenty-five environments fell within that range. Twenty were strong perturbations.
Near home, the ranking of mutants is largely preserved. IRA1 nonsense mutants stay on top.
lines.say: Near home, the ranking of mutants is largely preserved. I R A 1 nonsense mutants stay on top.

lines.t: Far from home, surprises appear. In salt, IRA1 and PDE2 mutants suffer, but GPB2 mutants do not. With long transfers, IRA1 nonsense mutants become deleterious.
lines.say: Far from home, surprises appear. In salt, I R A 1 and P D E 2 mutants suffer, but G P B 2 mutants do not. With long transfers, I R A 1 nonsense mutants become deleterious.

lines.t: Different fitness profiles imply different effects on phenotype. But how many phenotypes?
The trick is to treat fitness as a matrix, mutants by environments, and factor it with singular value decomposition.
Each mutant becomes a point in an abstract phenotype space. Each environment becomes a set of weights: how much each phenotype matters there.
Across the subtle environments, eight components rose above measurement noise. The first alone explained 95% of the variation.
lines.say: Across the subtle environments, eight components rose above measurement noise. The first alone explained ninety-five percent of the variation.

lines.t: Trained on just 60 mutants, the model predicted the other 232, including mutants in genes it had never seen.
lines.say: Trained on just sixty mutants, the model predicted the other two hundred thirty-two, including mutants in genes it had never seen.

lines.t: Then the real test: the strong environments. There, the eight-component model explained 29 to 95% of the variation.
lines.say: Then the real test: the strong environments. There, the eight-component model explained twenty-nine to ninety-five percent of the variation.

lines.t: In high salt, the first component alone does worse than guessing the average. With all eight, the model explains 72%.
lines.say: In high salt, the first component alone does worse than guessing the average. With all eight, the model explains seventy-two percent.

lines.t: Here is the twist. The three smallest components explained only about 1% of fitness variation near home.
lines.say: Here is the twist. The three smallest components explained only about one percent of fitness variation near home.

lines.t: Far away, they mattered: in the six-day transfer environment, they added nearly half of the explained variation.
Adaptive mutations, the authors conclude, are locally modular: they affect only a few traits that matter where they evolved.
But they are globally pleiotropic, carrying hidden side effects that surface in new environments.
Mutants that look alike today may answer tomorrow's challenges very differently. That matters for cancer, for infections, and for predicting evolution itself.
And it all rests on a simple idea: twenty random letters of DNA, copied faithfully, that let us count evolution as it happens.
